takeaway: EET finds DBMS logic bugs by replacing query expressions with semantically equivalent forms and flagging discrepancies between original and transformed executions, without restricting whole-query shape.
background: DBMS logic bugs silently return wrong rows or updates. Existing metamorphic or query-synthesis oracles constrain SQL shapes because they must reason about the whole query.
villain: Query-level manipulation cannot reliably model complex SQL semantics, so prior tools omit features such as correlated subqueries, joins, windows, or DML and miss bugs reached by those queries.
approach: EET generates SQL with SQLsmith, walks each query's AST, and transforms every supported expression while preserving semantics. Boolean expressions gain determined true or false subexpressions derived from SQL's three-valued logic; other types gain redundant CASE WHEN branches. It runs original and transformed queries, compares both outputs and database changes, and reduces mismatching pairs in stages.
impact: The authors argue that expression-level metamorphic testing broadens logic-bug detection to complex queries whose overall semantics need not be modeled.

evaluation.overview: The authors ran randomized tests on selected open-source engines, classified reported bugs, analyzed fixed bugs and SQL features, and compared bug age with prior techniques rather than rerunning those techniques.
evaluation.implemented: A fully automatic black-box C/C++ testing tool built on SQLsmith, including database/query generation, AST transformation, result and database-state comparison, and staged test-case reduction.
evaluation.setting: Development versions of MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, and TiDB ran on Ubuntu on an AMD EPYC host during an intermittent testing campaign.

results.text: Across the evaluated engines, the authors report 66 unique bugs: 65 confirmed and 37 fixed; 35 were logic bugs.
The authors traced 13 of the 35 logic bugs to versions released before 2020; the longest-latent bug had existed for 20 years.

limitations: EET assumes deterministic query results and therefore excludes SQL features involving randomness. As a metamorphic oracle, it misses bugs when original and transformed queries produce the same wrong result, and each SQL dialect may require its own branch syntax.
phd_group_signal: This work signals a testing-systems style combining logical equivalence, grammar-based generation, black-box differential checking, automatic reduction, and developer-confirmed bug reports.

claims.text: EET traverses a generated query's AST, replaces supported expressions with equivalents built from determined Boolean expressions or redundant CASE WHEN branches, and treats any difference in query output or database changes as a bug signal.
The soundness argument excludes nondeterministic SQL features, and the authors note that EET cannot detect a bug when both original and transformed queries return the same incorrect result.
